title: The young men in the cave
hook: young believers flee to a cave and pray, our Lord, grant us mercy and set right our affair (18:10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Kahf, the Friday surah, read for a week of light. Your line was friday's surah.

A handful of young men in a city where their faith has become dangerous. Their people, the surah says, have taken other gods beside the One. They can stay and pretend, or they can go. They go: past the edge of town, up into the hills, into a cave in the rock, with nothing but each other and a dog. And the first thing they do, once the noise is gone, is ask for something.

The Qur'an calls them fitya, young men. Verse thirteen says they believed in their Lord, and God increased them in guidance. Verse fourteen says God bound their hearts firm when they stood up and said: our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. Then they withdrew. And at the cave mouth, in Pickthall's translation of verse ten: "Our Lord! Give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight." Two halves. Mercy from Your presence: min ladunk, from with You, straight from God rather than from the people around them. And: arrange for us, out of our affair, rashad, a sound way through. They don't ask to win, or for their enemies to fall. They ask for mercy, and for their situation to be set straight. Then God puts them to sleep, which is tomorrow's story. The Qur'an doesn't name the city or the century. It mentions ar-Raqim, a word commentators explain in different ways: an inscribed tablet, a place, a valley. Christians tell a story of sleepers in a cave near Ephesus, and some Muslim commentators connected the two; the Qur'an leaves the details open, and warns, a few verses on, against arguing about them. What it keeps is the prayer. Muslims still say it, word for word in Arabic, when a situation is beyond them: rabbana atina min ladunka rahmah, wa hayyi' lana min amrina rashada. It's the prayer of people who did the one thing they could, which was to leave, and handed the rest over.
screen: `FITYA: YOUNG MEN, HEARTS MADE FIRM.` · `MERCY FROM YOUR PRESENCE.` · `SET OUR AFFAIR STRAIGHT.` · `NO CITY, NO CENTURY, NAMED.` · then, large: `SHAPE FOR US RIGHT CONDUCT IN OUR PLIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one tangled situation in your life, a job, a family knot, a decision with no clean answer, and picture yourself stepping out of it for a moment, the way they stepped into the cave. If you pray, you can say their du'a, in Arabic or your own language: our Lord, give us mercy from Your presence, and set right our affair. If you don't, just hold the situation without trying to fix it, and let it be held.
Fitya. The young men who left a city turned from God, and asked for mercy and a straight way through. Today's word.
Your line: set right our affair. Mercy first, then a way through. Day four hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: The du'a of 18:10 is memorized by Muslims and said in Arabic when facing a difficult situation; it's also recited as part of al-Kahf on Fridays.

chat.says: What did the young men in the cave pray for?
options: Mercy from God's presence, and for their situation to be set right.
For God to defeat the people of the city who had turned on them.
To be hidden asleep for centuries until the city changed its faith.
chat.meaning: 18:10: give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight. They don't ask to win.

min ladunk.meaning: from Your presence; straight from God

rashad.meaning: right conduct, a sound way through

ar-Raqim.meaning: a word in 18:9 explained as a tablet, place or valley

Ephesus.meaning: an ancient city where Christians place their cave sleepers
